inference_aids.alt: Evening in a small kitchen. Tessa stands between her husband Baldo, in the doorway with a sword at his belt, and her brother Lapo by the table.
inference_aids.art_brief: Florence, 2 May 1300, evening, the kitchen of Tessa and Baldo's small house at San Piero Maggiore, near the Donati houses. Low beams, a plain wooden table, bread and a jug on it, a hearth glowing at one side. Tessa (about 20, plain blue-grey dress, hair covered, tired and frightened) stands in the middle of the room with her back half to the table, between the two men. Lapo (16, plain dark tunic of a junior clerk) stands by the table, hands at his sides, looking at Baldo. Baldo (about 28, broad, a retainer of the Donati household, leather jerkin, sword in its scabbard at his belt) fills the open doorway from the street, laughing, at ease. Warm firelight on Tessa and Lapo, evening dusk behind Baldo. No coins on the table yet, no blood, no drawn weapon.

words_with_history.title: Dal latino all'italiano
words_with_history.note_en: The Latin future (*cantabo, habebo, dicam*) did not survive into Italian: in late Latin its forms had fallen together with others (*cantabit* and *cantavit* sounded almost alike). Speakers used instead, schematically, the infinitive with *habeo*, "I have to sing": *cantare habeo* became *canterò*, *dicere habeo* became *dirò*, and the endings of the future are the present of *avere*: *-ò, -ai, -à, -anno* are *ho, hai, ha, hanno*; *-emo, -ete* come from the old forms *avemo, avete* (Latin *habemus, habetis*), not from modern *abbiamo*. The Tuscan conditional joined the infinitive to a past of *habere*, *habui*: *cantare habui → canterei*, *dicere habuit → direbbe*. A second conditional, from the infinitive with *habebam* (*cantare habebam → canteria*; *saria, avria*), was the form of the Sicilian poets of Frederick II's court; through their verse it came into Tuscan poetry. Dante uses both; the modern language kept *-ei*. (Bindo's *saria* is this course's colouring for an old man's speech.) Words of the chapter: *debito* is *debitum*, "what is owed", the participle of *debere* (*dovere*), the same verb as in *deve dare*; *parente* comes from *parens*, but means any relative, not only a father or mother; *moglie* comes from *mulier*, "woman", which in Italian narrowed to "wife"; *comune* is *communis*, "shared": the Commune is the city as a thing its citizens hold in common; and *ufficio* is *officium*, "duty, service", which in late and medieval Latin came to mean a public post.

grammar.title: Dirò, direi
grammar.rule: Domani dirò, verrai, pagheranno · io direi, tu diresti, io aspetterei · saria = sarebbe · me lo, te lo, glielo, me li, ve li
grammar.note_en:
**The future.** Italian has a one-word future, as Latin does, but not the Latin one: it is built on the infinitive. Take the infinitive, drop the final *-e*, and add *-ò, -ai, -à, -emo, -ete, -anno*. Regular verbs in *-are* change their *a* to *e*: *aspettare → aspetterà* (will wait), *cercare → cercheranno* (they will look for), *pagare → pagheranno* (they will pay; the *h* keeps *c* and *g* hard). The irregular futures are mostly the same endings on a shortened or assimilated stem (*venir- → verr-*): *essere → sarò, sarà, saranno*; *avere → avrà, avremo*; *dire → dirò, dirai*; *venire → verrai, verrà*; *sapere → saprai, sapranno*; *rimanere → rimarrai, rimarranno*; *cadere → cadranno*; and, on the same pattern, *farà* (he will do), *vorrà* (he will want), *potrà* (he will be able), *dovrai* (you will have to) and *andrò* (I shall go).

**What the future does here.** It promises (*Non dirò niente a nessuno*, I shall say nothing to anyone), threatens (*Questi pagheranno*, these men will pay), predicts (*I Cerchi cadranno*, the Cerchi will fall) and gives quiet orders, as in English "you'll be here early": Bindo's *Domani verrai presto* (come early tomorrow). In this chapter the same future does several of these jobs at once. Lapo's *Te lo prometto. Non dirò niente a nessuno* is a promise; Baldo turns it round: *Lo so. Non lo dirai* (I know. You won't tell it), which is both trust and a threat. After *se* (if) and *quando* (when), for something still to come, Italian can use the future where English uses the present, as Latin does (*si scies, venies*, "if you know, you will come"); the present is also possible (*Se i Cerchi lo sanno…*, if the Cerchi find out): *Se ne saprai altri, verrai da me e me li dirai* (if you learn any more, you will come to me and tell me them); *Se messer Vieri lo saprà, che farà di me?* (if messer Vieri finds out, what will he do with me?).

**The conditional** (*condizionale*) is built on the same stem as the future, with the endings *-ei, -esti, -ebbe, -emmo, -este, -ebbero*: *direi, diresti* (I, you would say); *aspetterei, aspetterebbe* (I, he would wait); *sarebbe* (it would be); *riderebbero* (they would laugh). Latin has no single form for it: its nearest equivalents are the "potential" subjunctive, *dixerim* (I would say), *velim* (I would like), and *dicerem* (I would say) in a condition: a correspondence of use, not a one-to-one match. It gives an opinion or advice without insisting: the partner's *Io porterei i nomi alla Signoria* (I would take the names to the Signoria) and Lapo's *Ma io aspetterei* (but I would wait); it asks what someone would do: *Giureresti davanti ai priori che questi erano in piazza?* (would you swear before the priors that these men were in the square?) — *Lo giurerei* (I would swear it). It also tells what would follow: *Sarebbe un grande errore* (it would be a great mistake); *I Donati riderebbero di noi per cento anni* (the Donati would laugh at us for a hundred years). Lapo's *Io aspetterei* decides something in the shop: the names stay on Vieri's desk, and nobody asks him in front of the Signoria about the men on foot.

**Two pronouns together.** When an indirect object (to me, to you, to him) and a direct object (it, them) go together before the verb, the indirect comes first, and *mi, ti, ci, vi* become *me, te, ce, ve*: *me li dirai* (you will tell them to me), *ve li dirò* (I shall tell them to you), *Me lo prometti? Te lo prometto* (Do you promise me? I promise you). *Gli* or *le* with *lo, la, li, le* make one word: *glielo, gliela, glieli*: *il consiglio glieli darà* (the council will give them to him). Tessa's *Glielo dirai?* means "will you tell it to them", to the Cerchi: in speech *gli* often stands for "to them" too. Before *ha* or *ho*, *lo* loses its vowel: *niuno me l'ha domandato* (nobody has asked me).

**Older forms.** From this chapter the older forms of the second level appear, each glossed at its first use: *a'* (= *ai*, to the: *a' Cerchi*), *ne'* (= *nei*), *co'* (= *coi*), and the subject pronouns *egli* (he) and *ella* (she), the written forms of *lui* and *lei*. *De'* (= *dei*) and *niuno* (= *nessuno*) are already known. Bindo, the oldest man in the shop, says *Saria meglio* for *Sarebbe meglio* (it would be better): *saria* is the older conditional in *-ia*, a literary form that Dante still uses; in this course the old speakers use such forms as colouring. Read it; write *sarebbe*.

**The tables in English.** *Vieri aspetta sempre / Vieri aspetterà*: Vieri always waits / Vieri will wait. *Lo so / Non lo dirai*: I know / You won't tell it. *Te lo prometto / Non dirò niente a nessuno*: I promise you / I shall tell nobody anything. *Non hanno il suo nome / Se lo sapranno, lo cercheranno*: they haven't got his name / if they find out, they will look for him. *me li dirai*: you will tell them to me; *ve li dirò*: I shall tell them to you; *il consiglio glieli darà*: the council will give them to him; *niuno me l'ha domandato*: nobody has asked me. In the paradigm tables: *dirò* I shall say, *verrai* you will come, *saprai* you will learn, *saranno* they will be, *avrà* he will have, *avranno* they will have, *rimarrai* you will stay, *mentirò* I shall lie, *pagheranno* they will pay, *cadranno* they will fall; *direi* I would say, *giureresti* you would swear, *aspetterebbe* he would wait, *domanderebbe* he would ask, *riderebbero* they would laugh.

**Fact and fiction.** Cardinal Matteo d'Acquasparta came to Florence in early June 1300 as Boniface VIII's legate, to make peace between the parties, and he asked for a share of the city's offices for the pope's friends; he left in October. The priors who took office on 15 June 1300 for two months included Dante Alighieri; the chapter does not give the other names. Guido Cavalcanti, the poet, was a leader of the Cerchi side and an enemy of Corso Donati. The Cerchi kinsman, the partners, the list of six names and the crier's words are invented.

A.title: A
A.instruction: Block 1: write the verb in brackets in the future (items 1–2: a plan, a threat) or in the conditional (item 3: the answer keeps the tense of the question). Block 2: write the two pronouns (one word or two) that replace the words in brackets.

items.prompt: Il parente a Lapo: «Domani ___ (venire) da me con gli altri nomi.»
items.explanation: A plan for tomorrow, to tu: future of venire, irregular stem verr-: verrai.

items.prompt: Tessa ha paura: «Se i Cerchi lo sanno, ___ (cercare) mio marito.»
items.explanation: A threat she foresees: future, loro. cercare → cercheranno (h keeps the c hard).

items.prompt: «Davanti a messer Vieri lo giureresti?» «Sì, lo ___ (giurare).»
items.explanation: An answer to a question in the conditional: io giurerei (would swear).

common_wrong.hint: The question asks what he would do: answer in the conditional.

items.prompt: Lapo al parente: «Gli altri nomi? ___ dirò, messere.» (a voi + li)
items.explanation: Lapo gives voi to the kinsman: vi + li → ve li.

B.title: B
B.instruction: Complete each sentence with a word from the bank, unchanged. Four words are not used.

items.prompt: Il papa manda a Firenze un cardinale a fare la pace per lui: è il suo ___.
Chi deve dare dieci fiorini a un amico ha con lui un ___ di dieci fiorini.

C.title: C
C.instruction: Questions 1–2: answer in Italian or in English, in your own words, then compare with the model answer. Questions 3–4, Dal latino all'italiano: write the standard Italian form. (3) The Italian future is the infinitive + habeo: dicere habeo, 'I have to say', became 'I shall say'; write it for io. (4) The conditional in -ia comes from the infinitive + habebat (late Latin *essere habebat → saria); write the standard form for 'it would be'.

items.prompt: Che cosa fece Lapo con i fiorini di Baldo?
model_answers: Lapo prese un fiorino e lo pesò nella mano, come ser Bindo. Non era scarso, ma Lapo lo mise di nuovo sulla tavola e lasciò lì i tre fiorini.
items.rubric: Baldo put three florins on the table "for supper", after thanking Lapo and promising to speak of him to his master. Lapo weighed one in his hand as Bindo weighs coin (it was full weight), put it back and took none; Tessa did not take them either. A full answer says that he weighed one and that he did not keep them.

items.prompt: Perché Lapo disse al socio: «Io aspetterei»?
model_answers: Perché davanti alla Signoria qualcuno domanderebbe anche de' fanti, e Lapo non voleva dire il nome di Baldo.
items.rubric: The young partner wanted to take the six names to the Signoria, with Lapo repeating them there. Lapo thought that before the Signoria someone would also ask about the men on foot, and Baldo was one of them. So he advised waiting, like Vieri, and the names stayed on Vieri's desk. Bindo saw why. An answer that says only "because he was cautious" misses Baldo.

items.prompt: Lapo a Tessa: «Il nome di Baldo? Non lo ___ a nessuno.» (dire, io)
items.explanation: dicere habeo → dirò: the infinitive dire, shortened, + -ò (from habeo, ho).

items.prompt: Ser Bindo dice «Saria meglio». Lapo dice: «___ meglio.»
items.explanation: saria (from habebat) is the older literary conditional; the standard form, from habuit, is sarebbe.

vocabulary.current_sense: prior (one of the city's six governors)

provenance.author: Claude Opus 5.5 (swarm writer, chapter 5)
provenance.review_required: Draft. Two GPT-6.1 Sol critique rounds, one Codex review (GPT-6.1 Sol, high) and a fresh-eyes Claude Opus review; findings addressed as recorded in the notes.
reviewers: GPT-6.1 Sol via Codex (single chapter review, cx job 1108-185636-6856, 2026-11-08)
notes: Length: about 1,580 running words (window 1,500–2,000), five sections; every card beat is staged with a turn. Scenes were deepened after the first critique (the Cerchi men at Tessa's door, Lapo's 'Io aspetterei' before the Signoria, Bindo's 'Ti metterà fuori…'), not padded.

Written in the parallel wave (chapters 2–7 at once). The plan rows of chapters 2–4 are treated as known; inflected forms of their lexemes first met here (e.g. pagheranno, cercheranno, aspetterei, sedeva, taciuto) are declared in this delta under the plan chapter's first_lesson, with each form dated to lesson 5.

New lexemes: the 29 planned plus one writer addition within the ceiling (30 of 95): it-giugno (three uses). it-piede (a piedi) was dropped at integration: chapter 4 introduced it first (lower chapter wins); its forms here are all already in chapter 4's entry. Words owned by later chapters were written around (dì and partire ch6, via ch14, solo ch8, famiglia ch12, morte/fine unassigned and avoided).

The held deltas of chapters 8 and 15 already date this chapter's shared words (sperare, dormire, meglio, piacere, ringraziare, giurare, aiuto, onore, parente, rimanere, tale, promettere, nascondere, ufficio, fratello) to lesson 5 with no base card stage (2026-11-08 consolidation); their sense ids and glosses are copied here exactly, so the held files needed no edit.

Shared-file edits: course.json bridge_references.la appended dicere habeo, dicere habui, Iunius, placet, auxilium (real Latin forms in the sense used); the lesson index row now has path instead of planned_path (published false, status draft). glosses/forms.json: 79 new keys, and the story senses of legato (legate) and signoria (the Signoria) put before the v3 defaults. Per-lesson phrase layer glosses/capitolo-05.json (faccia = face, sono corso, se ne andò, prima o poi, guardare dall'alto…).

Register: level 2 begins. Each older form is glossed at its first use here (a' = ai, ne' = nei, co' = coi, ella = lei, egli = lui, saria = sarebbe), since a parallel writer cannot know whether a neighbour glossed it first. saria occurs once, in Bindo's mouth; its standard twin sarebbe occurs in the prose and is the answer of the Dal latino item. coi (the twin of co') is declared incidental. dì is not used: chapter 6 plans it as a word.

Exercise placement (course convention): ten items, A 4 (future, conditional, combined pronouns: each answer a cell the prose shows), B 2, C 2 story questions + 2 Dal latino items as the last block of Pensa C, with the Latin cues in C's English instruction.

History: Matteo d'Acquasparta arrives in early June 1300 (research table, verified) and is named in the prose only as messer Matteo, cardinal and legate; his request for a share of the offices follows the card. The priors of 15 June – 14 August 1300 include Dante (verified); the other five are not named; the crier's wording, the Cerchi kinsman, the two partners and the six names are invented, as the grammar note's Fact and fiction paragraph says.
The Cerchi kinsman is not named (chapter 4, written in parallel, may name him): speaker char-cerchi-kinsman from continuity.json. The two partners are unnamed extras with chapter-scoped speaker ids.
continuity warning: the chapter's continuity-log entries are merged into continuity.json at finalize.

Sol round 1 (prose): fixed the oath idiom (now «Giureresti davanti ai priori che erano in piazza?»), Tessa's threat («Gli taglieranno il naso, come a Ricoverino»), and deleted the narrator's verdict «Lapo non mentì»; added pressure at Tessa's door, «E gli altri non li vedesti?», Baldo's «Domani parlerò di te al mio padrone», and made Lapo's «Ma io aspetterei» decide that the names stay on Vieri's desk.

Sol round 2 (full chapter): removed solo (chapter 8's word) and se ne andò (G07, receptive later); rewrote Bindo's objectless «Lo spero per lei» and the partner's «Chi li pagherà» (nose and honour), dropped an unmotivated torneranno/riderebbero switch; qualified the se/quando rule (the future is possible, the present too); -emo/-ete traced to old avemo/avete (habemus, habetis), not abbiamo; removed the claim that the -ia conditional entered old men's speech; Pensa A now states the tense of each item; translations added for every table sentence and form list.

Codex review: (1) contextual tap-gloss corrections in glosses/capitolo-05.json for every ambiguous occurrence (object lo/l', gli 'to him', numeral sei, verso 'towards', vicino 'near', loro 'their', lei 'she', parte 'a share', consiglio 'advice', presto 'early', fra 'in', interrogative che, sono corso and case grandi with components), checked through core.glossAt; forms.json gained the missing alternative senses and presto's adverb now comes before the v3 'lend'. (2) The grammar note's futures are now all from the prose (farà, vorrà, potrà, dovrai, andrò; potrà, dovrai and andrò were worked into existing lines). (3) Relative che clauses (G06) were rephrased out (s008, s134, s152, s168, s172); complement che (dice che…, giureresti che…) and the free relative chi already used in chapter 1 remain. (4) «I nuovi priori sono uomini del popolo» now names its referent, so Cavalcanti, a magnate, is not called a popolano. Suggestions taken: meglio glossed at its first use, the A worked example labelled leggere → leggerà, the Latin derivations marked schematic.

Fresh-eyes review (no blockers): fixed «che questi erano in piazza» (no relative misreading), «Tessa li guardò, ma non li prese» (for anche lei non), «tra la gente c'era Gherardo» (they had not met since May), meglio now glossed melius (bridge string appended) instead of più bene, «Li dirò, messere, se messer Vieri lo vorrà» (no conditional with se + present), the same night's sighting now in the passato prossimo («Questi li ho visti bene»; «non li hai visti?»), Pensa B without give-away English cues, c03 now Lapo's own promise to Tessa, «due soci», «disse il più vecchio», «Con un legato tale», «di nuovo» for ancora, «a casa di sua sorella», «Parla il tuo orgoglio, non i conti», «Cavalcanti so chi è», one sentence per segment at the end, English of the note, avremo dropped from the table, c01 model answer, officium's sense shift in Dal latino.
Prior coverage sits at the part-2 floor (85%); one sentence of known words closes section 1 («Fino alla mattina, nella strada, passarono uomini con le armi»), echoing its opening.
melius appended to course.json bridge_references.la (with dicere habeo, dicere habui, Iunius, placet, auxilium).

Integration (rebase on origin/main 741bba8, chapters 2–4 published): forms of chapter 1–4 lexemes that those chapters already introduced were removed from this delta; only forms first seen here remain, dated to lesson 5. course.json and glosses/forms.json conflicts resolved by union (origin's entries plus this chapter's bridge strings, index row and gloss keys).

review_questions.quote: Sulle sue mani c'era ancora sangue.
review_questions.question: [?] Chapter 4 (written in parallel) stages the kinsman's arrival; is a kinsman with blood on his hands compatible with it?
review_questions.resolution: Integration: chapter 4's continuity log has the kinsman with blood on his hands and clothes, not his own. Consistent.

review_questions.quote: Quella sera io ero qui, alla finestra.
review_questions.question: [?] Bindo saw Baldo from the shop window as the Donati men came home past the shop: this depends on chapter 4 keeping Bindo in the shop that evening (its card: he has closed the shutters).
review_questions.resolution: Integration: chapter 4 keeps Bindo in the shuttered shop watching the street from the window (he counts the fanti at messer Vieri's door). Consistent.

review_questions.quote: Dalla festa di maggio Lapo non lo vedeva.
review_questions.question: [?] Lapo and Gherardo first meet again in mid-June; chapters 4 and 6 (parallel) should not stage an earlier meeting.
review_questions.resolution: Integration: chapter 4 separates Lapo and Gherardo in the crush and does not reunite them; coordinator confirmed. Consistent.

review_questions.question: [?] glielo with gli = 'to them' (the Cerchi), colloquial; the grammar note says so. Acceptable for period-flavoured dialogue?
review_questions.resolution: Codex: acceptable under the course's standard-Italian dialogue; plural gli is valid informal usage and the note names its referent.

review_questions.quote: Pochi giorni dopo, in una mattina di giugno
review_questions.question: [?] Fresh-eyes suggested the vaguer «In quei giorni». Kept «Pochi giorni dopo»: the legate arrives in early June and the priors take office on 15 June, so the interval between the shop scene and the proclamation is at most about ten days.
review_questions.resolution: Writer: kept; the interval is bounded by the verified dates.

review_questions.question: [?] Fresh-eyes suggested replacing the form note desti = hai dato with a tense label. Kept: the note equates the remoto of Tuscan speech with its modern spoken twin, as the course's G03 note does, and the English reveal names the tense.

review_questions.quote: e il legato avrà poca pace
review_questions.question: [?] Fresh-eyes found «avrà poca pace» slightly ambiguous (his peace or his peace-making). Kept: in context it reads as 'will have little success with his peace', and it supplies the avrà table cell.
